meta: Kubo Shunman's hanging scroll of a Chinese palace lady with a fan before a banana plant, possibly an allusion to Lady Ban.
about: A Chinese palace lady holds a round fan and stands before a banana plant. The poem at the top is in kanbun, a Japanese way of writing Chinese. The Cleveland Museum thinks its imagery of a palanquin, silk fan and autumn winds may allude to Lady Ban, a consort who lost an emperor's favour. In a poem attributed to her, Ban compared herself to a used silk fan put away in autumn. Ukiyo-e artists, the museum adds, extended their interest in beautiful people to figures from other lands.

meta: Richard Parkes Bonington's The Grand Canal, painted in Venice in 1826 or 1827, with Gothic palazzi and a distant bridge.
about: Gothic-arched palazzi line the left side of a sunlit Grand Canal, with moored boats and a red-draped cargo in front and a distant bridge and bell tower closing the view. Richard Parkes Bonington painted it in 1826 or 1827. It belonged first to his father, who sold it at Christie's in London. Welbore Ellis Agar, 2nd Earl of Normanton, took it home to Somerley, and it stayed in the family until the 6th Earl consigned it to a New York dealer. The National Gallery of Art bought it in 2001.
credit_line: Gift of Victoria and Roger Sant

meta: Jean François Raffaëlli's Notre Dame de Paris, about 1890, with two nuns on a wet quay, once owned by Potter Palmer of Chicago.
about: Two nuns in black habits walk along the water's edge below Notre Dame, seen across a wet quay lined with bare trees. An old man and his dog sit under the trees. Jean François Raffaëlli painted it about 1890. An inventory in the Art Institute archives says Potter Palmer of Chicago owned it by 1893. His widow Bertha Honoré Palmer had it next, and then their sons Honoré and Potter. They gave it to the Art Institute in 1922.

meta: Nicholas Chevalier's painting of the wedding of Prince Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, in St Petersburg on 23 January 1874.
about: A bride in a white gown with a fur-trimmed train stands before a priest in gold vestments in an ornate church, with officers and ladies looking on. The wedding took place in the Imperial Chapel of the Winter Palace in St Petersburg. Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, fourth child of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert, married Grand Duchess Marie, a daughter of Tsar Alexander II. In the picture the couple hold candles. The Metropolitan Archbishop who conducted the ceremony holds a cross above them, and six Chamberlains carry the bride's train. Nicholas Chevalier painted it in 1874 and 1875.

meta: Etienne Delaune's engraved design for the back of a hand mirror with scenes from the story of Medea, about 1560.
about: The back of a hand mirror carries a central scene of Medea fleeing Corinth in a chariot drawn by winged dragons, which belonged to her grandfather Helios. Below, she makes Jason's father Aeson young again. The frame is crowded with strapwork and female figures, with an enthroned woman at the top and pearls hanging down each side. Etienne Delaune made the design as an engraving about 1560, for a craftsman to copy in metal.

meta: Jacques de Gheyn II's Venus and Amor, 1605, a painting that once belonged to the Dutch stadholders.
about: Venus sits naked on a cloth on the ground, holding a burning heart in her left hand with her right arm across the shoulders of Amor. He is about to shoot an arrow. Two doves mate at lower left, and a few flowers lie on the cloth. The Rijksmuseum notes that the picture came from the stadholders' collection, and the arms of Stadholder-King William III are fixed to the back. Jacques de Gheyn II painted it in 1605.

meta: Alphonse Mucha's 1894 poster for Victorien Sardou's play Gismonda with Sarah Bernhardt, at the Théâtre de la Renaissance in Paris.
about: Alphonse Mucha made this tall poster for Victorien Sardou's play Gismonda, which opened on 31 October 1894 at the Théâtre de la Renaissance in Paris. Sarah Bernhardt starred. A woman in a golden robe wears a pink floral crown and holds a green palm frond, framed by an arched mosaic background. The lettering imitates mosaic too. Wikipedia describes the play as a Greek-set melodrama in four acts. The National Gallery Prague holds the work.

meta: John Hoppner's The Hoppner Children, 1791: three children by a stream in an autumn wood, later in the Widener collection.
about: Three children are shown in an autumn wood beside a stream, with a boy in a red suit and white ruffled collar standing over two younger ones near the water. John Hoppner painted them in 1791. After the artist's wife died, the picture passed to her sons, the last of them Richard Belgrave Hoppner. It sold at Christie's in London in 1893 under the title The Hoppner Children and soon reached the American collector Peter A. B. Widener. Joseph E. Widener gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1942.

meta: A portrait of Pocahontas as an English lady, catalogued under Simon van de Passe, at the National Portrait Gallery in Washington.
about: An oval portrait shows a young woman in a red gown with gold embroidery, a black hat and a large lace collar, holding a feather fan. The painting follows an engraving made at the time of her visit and presents Pocahontas as an affluent Englishwoman. The Smithsonian text says an English sea captain kidnapped her in 1613. In captivity she took the name Rebecca and married John Rolfe. The Virginia Company brought her to England in June 1616 to publicize her apparent assimilation to investors.

meta: Juan Gris's Ace of Clubs and Four of Diamonds, 1915: a cubist still life of playing cards, once owned by John Quinn.
about: Fragmented playing cards, including an ace of clubs and red diamond shapes, overlap with planes of blue, green, brown and black. A glass-like form and a patterned cloth sit at the centre. John Quinn of New York owned the picture, and it was sold from his estate at the Hôtel Drouot in Paris in 1926. It went to the dealer Jeanne Bucher and then to her son-in-law, Dr. André Cournand. Robert and Mercedes Eichholz bought it in 1966 and left it to the National Gallery of Art.
credit_line: Gift of Robert and Mercedes Eichholz

meta: Isaac Israels's 1890 painting of two Amsterdam maidservants chatting on the Leidsegracht, bequeathed to the Rijksmuseum.
about: Two Amsterdam maidservants in aprons and white caps stand talking on the Leidsegracht. The Rijksmuseum notes the house numbers 10 to 14 in the background, running from right to left. Isaac Israels painted it in oil on card in 1890. From 1919 it hung in the museum on loan from Jean Charles Joseph Drucker and Maria Lydia Drucker-Fraser of Montreux, together with many other paintings. Their bequest made it the museum's own in 1944.

meta: Nicolaes Maes's Portrait of a Lady, signed in 1676, a seated woman in red velvet with pearls and a sunset behind her.
about: A seated woman in a red velvet dress with white sleeves wears a golden shawl and a double strand of pearls, with a dark curtain and a sunset landscape behind her. Nicolaes Maes signed it in 1676. The museum calls her only a lady, but when the picture was sold in Amsterdam in 1926 it was catalogued as a portrait of Johanna Koerten, wife of Adriaan Blok. Earlier it was in the Camberlyn d'Amougies collection near Brussels. Joseph F. McCrindle gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 2001.

meta: Asher B. Durand's 1830 oval portrait of Mary Louisa Adams, born in the White House while her grandfather was president.
about: Mary Louisa Adams was born in the White House in 1828, while her grandfather John Quincy Adams was president. Asher Durand painted her in an oval portrait in 1830, in a white off-shoulder dress tied with blue bows. The museum says he emphasized her rosy cheeks and conveyed a more reserved personality than her younger sister Georgianna Frances. A portrait of the sister is also in the same collection.

meta: William Merritt Chase's A Friendly Call, 1895: his wife Alice talks with a visitor in the studio at Shinnecock Hills.
about: Two women talk in a richly decorated studio, one seated on a green-draped sofa in a white dress and wide hat with a pink parasol. Wikipedia identifies the hostess as Chase's wife Alice and says the room is the studio of their summer house at Shinnecock Hills, Long Island, rendered accurately when compared with a contemporary photograph. Samuel T. Shaw bought the picture in 1895 after it won the 1,500 dollar Shaw Fund prize at the Society of American Artists. Chester Dale gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1943.

meta: Ingres's Pope Pius VII in the Sistine Chapel, shown at the Salon of 1814 and commissioned by his friend and patron Marcotte.
about: A white-robed pope stands on a red-carpeted platform under a gilded canopy while cardinals and clergy gather around him in the Sistine Chapel. Wikipedia says Pius VII had been detained by Napoleon, so Ingres stressed his restored authority. Charles Marcotte, a friend and patron of the artist, commissioned the picture. The Salon of 1814 was the first after the Bourbon restoration. The signature now reads 1810, but the museum says the last digit was erased and falsely restored. It first read 1814.

meta: Thomas Eakins's Baby at Play, 1876: a toddler crouches on a brick floor stacking blocks, once owned by the artist's sister.
about: A young child in a white lace-trimmed dress and striped stockings crouches on a brick floor, stacking wooden blocks. Alphabet cubes and a red ball lie nearby. The picture stayed in Thomas Eakins's family at first, with his sister Mrs. William J. Crowell and then her son James. Dealers sold it on, and in 1954 John Hay Whitney bought it. His charitable trust gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1982.

meta: Johann Theodor de Bry's engraved pendant design with the figure of Fides, plate 2 of a series of eight, dated 1610.
about: A pendant with scroll motifs and hanging pear-shaped pearls frames Fides, shown as a nude woman with drapery holding a cross and a book. The museum wonders if the book is a Bible. Around the pendant are blackwork ornaments for enamelists, mostly options for the top and sides of rings. Johann Theodor de Bry engraved this as the second plate of a series of eight pendant designs.

meta: Jacques-Louis David's 1813 portrait Madame David, left by the sitter to her daughter and later bought by the Kress Foundation.
about: Marguerite-Charlotte David, born Pécoul, sits in a white satin gown with puffed sleeves and a red shawl over her arm. Jacques-Louis David signed the portrait in 1813. When she died in 1826 she left it to her daughter Laure, Baroness Meunier, in Calais. It then passed down through her descendants until the late 1940s. Dealers in Paris and New York held it next, and the Samuel H. Kress Foundation bought it in 1954.

meta: Bernardo Bellotto's The Fortress of Königstein, one of five views commissioned by Augustus III between 1756 and 1758.
about: The fortress of Königstein sits on a steep rocky plateau above green slopes, with figures resting beside grazing cattle in the foreground. Augustus III, king of Poland and elector of Saxony, commissioned Bernardo Bellotto to paint five views of it between 1756 and 1758. All were on canvases of the same size. They were meant to complete earlier views of Dresden and Pirna in the wing of the palace that housed the royal paintings. The Seven Years' War interrupted the work, and the paintings never reached the king.

meta: Thomas Sully's full-length portrait of Captain Charles Stewart, painted in 1811 and 1812 and bought by the National Gallery in 1947.
about: A naval captain stands full-length in a dark navy uniform with gold braid, holding a rolled document and a sword beside a table draped in red with books and a quill. Thomas Sully painted Captain Charles Stewart in 1811 and 1812. The picture went to Stewart's daughter Delia Stewart Parnell, then to her son Charles Stewart Parnell. Later owners in Boston lent it to the Museum of Fine Arts there for a long time. The National Gallery of Art purchased it in 1947.
